problem: Modular ObjectNav methods fuse the accumulated BEV spatial layout and temporal pose trajectory with plain CNNs. Because of CNN local bias, these ignore long-range spatio-temporal dependencies, causing state misperception and failed episodes despite extensive exploration.
motivation: Discriminative agent state representations are essential for long-term goal decisions in ObjectNav. Fig. 1 shows a CNN-based agent exploring widely yet never finding the target. Explicit cues about promising exploration regions (frontiers) and target-related regions should help.
key_idea: Encode spatial layout, temporal pose and a newly built passable frontier map separately, then use cross-attention decoders (spatial-frontier and temporal-pose) to produce frontier and target-related weights that enhance the state representation for a PPO long-term goal policy.
insight: Simply swapping the CNN for a ViT does not help (Tab. 3: ViT variants Φ3/Φ4 have lower SR than CNN Φ2/Φ1 despite lower value loss). Gains come from explicit decoders: NE-only is worse than CNN Φ2 (78.4 vs 79.7 Gibson SR), while adding SF and TP decoders together gives 82.6 (Tab. 4). The frontier decoder mainly improves SR and reduces exploration failures, whereas the pose decoder favors SPL. Adding the frontier map helps both CNN and ViT.
method: Passable frontier map: contour extraction gives the outer edge of the occupancy map; subtracting the obstacle map gives candidate frontiers; each is scored by S=A_f+λ·dist (distance term zeroed beyond threshold D) and low-scoring ones are discarded to form M^f

Navigation encoder: three conv sub-encoders E1/E2/E3 encode the frontier map, spatial layout (occupancy, obstacle, object semantic maps) and temporal pose (trajectory + current location maps concatenated with the replicated target semantic embedding)
Feature preprocessing: positional encoding, then self-attention on the spatial and pose features (not the frontier feature)
Spatial frontier (SF) decoder: cross-attention with frontier feature as query and spatial layout as key gives the critical frontier weight W^f
Temporal pose (TP) decoder: cross-attention with spatial layout as query and pose feature as key gives target-related weight W^s
State fusion: s_t = ē_t + softmax(W^f+W^s) ē_t w_v; an MLP outputs a distribution over 8 map-edge candidate points as the long-term goal
Policy: Fast Marching Method plans the path to the goal with a local policy; trained with PPO using success and exploration rewards; Stubborn's untrap mode is used

setting.backbone: NaviFormer (conv encoders + self/cross-attention decoders + MLP, trained with PPO from scratch); RedNet and Mask-RCNN for semantic segmentation
setting.training_data: Gibson (25 train scenes, tiny split), HM3D (80 train scenes), MP3D (56 train scenes); no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (4x480x640) plus pose; BEV maps 480x480
setting.action_space: long-term goal chosen among 8 map-edge points, executed by FMM planning with discrete actions (forward 0.25 m, turn 30°, stop)
setting.privileged: none (semantic segmentation predicted by RedNet/Mask-RCNN; pose is given)

results: NaviFormer beats SGM in SR by 4.6/1.5/2.4 points on Gibson/HM3D/MP3D (82.6/61.3/40.1 vs 78.0/59.8/37.7). It has the best SPL on HM3D and MP3D, but Gibson SPL (40.9) is below SGM (44.0). It also beats LLM/VLM zero-shot methods (ESC, L3MVN, PixNav) in SR and runs about 2-3x faster (8 FPS).
limitations: Gibson SPL (40.9) is lower than SGM (44.0), and MP3D DTS is worse than several baselines
Peanut and SGM were re-implemented under the authors' setup, and evaluation subsets differ from standard benchmarks, so comparisons are not fully standard
Relies on predicted semantic segmentation and given pose; only simulator evaluation, with no real-robot tests
